newsitem.title: UK: Panama launches ambitious search for investors.
newsitem.headline: Panama launches ambitious search for investors.

text.p: Tiny Central American republic Panama announced on Thursday big plans to use the return of the strategically located Panama Canal to local control to attract foreign direct investment.

Panama's former president Nicolas Ardito Barletta, while visiting London, unveiled the ambitious plan to develop his country's resources three years before Washington relinquishes control of the canal and its military installations.

"Panama is back on a democratic track and a new national effort is underway to advance the development of the country," Barletta, now administrator general of Panama's interoceanic region authority, told London investors.
"As we prepare for recovery of the canal in 1999, Panama is applying a strategic approach to modernising it and developing its unexploited opportunities."
Panama has put behind it the era of General Manuel Noriega, ousted in the 1989 U.S. invasion, and serving a 40-year sentence for his 1992 conviction on drug and racketeering charges.
Under Panama's fledgling democracy the canal will be sheltered from political interference, Barletta said.
He identified four key areas in which Panama was seeking international participation, either through joint ventures or foreign direct investment.

These entail the improvement of the canal itself, development of manufacturing for export, tourism, and the creation of a "city of knowledge" by inviting international research institutes to locate there.
Barletta said these projects would require foreign investment of at least $500 million in the next four years, and would require considerable infractructure support as well.
But plans to fit the canal for an increased volume of ocean-going traffic in the 21st century were top of his list.
"Changes bringing China and India into the world economy, and the opening up of Latin America and the former Soviet countries, will have a huge impact on shipping and on the Panama canal," he said.
A five year project to widen the narrowest part of the canal has already been elaborated, and Panama is keen to build a third set of locks for $7 billion on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts.
"The project may start in 2005 rather than 2010," Barletta said. "It is a very critical aspect for the Panama Canal."
The plan, outlined in 1991, would allow ships of up to 150,000 tonnes, rather than 65,000 tonnes as at present, into the 50-mile water-way that links the world's two great oceans.

While privatisation of the ports is already underway, Barletta said Panama would like to double the amount of fuel it provides to the 14,000 ships that pass annually through the canal. Panama currently provides 20 percent of their needs.
It also wants to protect and cultivate its water catchment areas since it provides millions of gallons to each vessel.
With some 22 percent of ships passing empty one way through the canal, Balletta said Panama would also like to see the establishment of cargo storing and loading facilities.
The creation of manufacturing zones for export goods was also a priority along with planned growth in tourism.

"The emphasis in the first instance will be the attraction of cruise ship tourists," he said. "The canal is the number one attraction but the ships don't stop in Panama because we don't have the facilities for their passengers."
